title: Bangladeshi Nakshi Kantha
facts: This is a nakshi kantha, a traditional embroidered quilt from Bengal, made by hand-stitching together several layers of old, worn cotton cloth.
The word kantha refers to the running-stitch technique itself, while nakshi comes from the Bengali word naksha, meaning artistic pattern or design, so nakshi kantha means a patterned kantha.

A kantha is traditionally made from old cotton saris and dhotis that have become too worn to wear, layered five to seven sheets thick and stitched together, turning worn-out cloth into something new and useful.
The embroidery thread was traditionally pulled out thread by thread from the colorful borders of those same old saris, so the stitching and the base cloth came from the very same recycled garments.
The simple running stitch used throughout a kantha causes the layered cloth to pucker and ripple very slightly as it is sewn, giving finished kanthas their soft, slightly wavy, textured surface.
Nakshi kanthas are traditionally made by rural women in Bengal, especially in areas like Jessore, Faridpur, and Rajshahi, often worked on together during long evenings as a shared, social craft.

A very common motif is a large lotus flower stitched at the center of the quilt, often understood to represent the universe or the sun, surrounded by trees of life, birds, fish, animals, and scenes of everyday village life.

Beyond bedding, kanthas were historically made for many everyday and ceremonial uses, including wrapping cloths for books and mirrors, cushion covers, and gifts given at weddings and other family occasions.
This particular craft tradition is recognized as centuries old, with references to kantha embroidery appearing in Bengali literature and folk life going back hundreds of years.
Nakshi kantha has seen a strong modern revival, with Bangladeshi designers and artisan cooperatives bringing the traditional stitching into contemporary clothing, bags, and home textiles.
The basic stitch is a simple running stitch, small and straight, though more elaborate nakshi kanthas add other stitches for outlining and shading the figures and motifs.
Kantha making was traditionally passed down from mother to daughter as a hands-on skill without written patterns, so each finished quilt's exact design was original to the woman who made it.
A large, densely embroidered nakshi kantha can take a woman several months of steady evening work to finish by hand.
The stitching is traditionally done without an embroidery hoop or frame, with the layered cloth simply held and worked directly in the maker's lap.

During the early twentieth-century Bengali cultural revival, elite and urban patrons, including circles connected to the poet Rabindranath Tagore, helped bring kantha embroidery attention as a serious folk art rather than only a household craft.
Beyond West Bengal in India and Jessore, Faridpur, and Rajshahi in Bangladesh, the kantha tradition has regional centers on both sides of the Bengal border, each with slightly different motif styles.
Some scholars trace the word kantha back to a Sanskrit word for rags or patched cloth, reflecting the technique's origin in reusing worn-out garments rather than buying new fabric.
Today, cooperatives and non-profit organizations in Bangladesh train and employ rural women in kantha embroidery, turning the traditional craft into a source of independent income.
Modern kantha work has expanded from quilts into sarees, scarves, bags, and fashion garments, sold both locally and exported internationally as part of Bangladesh's textile industry.

Because each kantha was originally made from whatever old saris a family had on hand, no two traditional kanthas are ever exactly alike in their base fabric, color palette, or exact stitching pattern.
